documents.title: AI for Students
documents.summary: Student-facing AI Hub page with study tips for using AI as a search, summary and study aid. It says policies differ by instructor and tells students to ask when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: "AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments" and "Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!" hand the decision to instructors, while only encouraging experimentation within academic policies.

units.why: "Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems" welcomes student use, so default permit/encourage (P02); it is bounded by academic policies, hence the fit note.
units.anchor: Experiment extensively with AI tools to learn and solve problems
units.fit_note: Encouragement is qualified by keeping NC State academic policies in mind.

units.why: "Know which tools are available and which tools are not" points students to the university approved/rejected tool list; closest is vetted-tool preference (P50), though no data rationale is given.
units.anchor: Know which tools are available and which tools are not.
units.fit_note: Only says to know the approved and rejected tools; no mention of data protection.

units.why: "Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI strengths and weaknesses" is advice on how to learn about AI; it matches no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Focus on familiar subjects to better understand AI’s strengths and weaknesses.
units.uncovered_note: Advice to test AI on familiar subjects to learn its strengths and weaknesses.

units.why: "rely on them with caution" followed by limited data, no true understanding and hallucination risk tells students to treat AI search output skeptically, which is P31.
units.anchor: rely on them with caution

units.why: "Be aware of the tool tendency to invent information" names hallucination, so students must verify (P31).
units.anchor: Be aware of the tool’s tendency to invent information.

units.why: "Summaries (like abstracts) can aid prioritization" allows AI summaries as a starting point; a study aid use (P14).
units.anchor: Summaries (like abstracts) can aid prioritization and initial comprehension.

units.why: "Writing your notes significantly improves long-term understanding" gives the reason to do the work yourself rather than outsource it (P41).
units.anchor: Writing your notes significantly improves long-term understanding.

units.why: "Use AI to generate quizzes, not just summaries" recommends AI-made practice quizzes (P14).
units.anchor: Use AI to generate quizzes, not just summaries.

units.why: "create practice questions for active learning and retrieval practice" is a recommended study use (P14).
units.anchor: Utilize LLMs to create practice questions for active learning and retrieval practice.

units.why: "Employ LLMs as a study aid, not a replacement for core materials" allows study-aid use with a limit; closest P14, the limit on replacing core materials is extra.
units.anchor: Employ LLMs as a study aid, not a replacement for core materials and reliable sources.
units.fit_note: Adds that AI must not replace core materials and reliable sources.

units.why: "Use LLMs to spark discussion and debate, not just passively accept summaries" asks students to stay active thinkers; P32 fits, though it is framed as a use suggestion.
units.anchor: Use LLMs to spark discussion and debate, not just passively accept summaries.
units.fit_note: Also recommends a specific use (sparking discussion and debate).

units.why: "Using AI for assignments may be heavily restricted by course policies" tells students rules are set by courses (P04) and warns of restriction.
units.anchor: Using AI for assignments may be heavily restricted by course policies.

units.why: "Direct problem-solving and writing are crucial for skill development" is rationale that doing the work builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: Direct problem-solving and writing are crucial for skill development.

units.why: "Receiving and responding to questions improves writing more effectively than direct editing" is pedagogical evidence for limiting AI editing; nearest is P41 but it is not about outsourcing practice.
units.anchor: Receiving and responding to questions improves writing more effectively than direct editing.
units.fit_note: Claims feedback by questions beats direct editing for writing; does not directly name AI.

units.why: "Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use" says fundamentals come first (P42).
units.anchor: Most courses emphasize developing a strong foundation before advanced tool use.

units.why: "AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments" says the rule is set per instructor or assignment (P04).
units.anchor: AI usage policies differ between instructors, courses and assignments.

units.why: "These policies aim to help you master fundamental and advanced skills" explains that course policies protect skill-building (P41).
units.anchor: These policies aim to help you master fundamental and advanced skills within your field.

units.why: "Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!" is a direct ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: Unsure about AI usage? Ask your instructor!

units.why: The page points students to LinkedIn Learning AI courses, an offered AI-literacy resource (P70).
units.anchor: you can find courses on LinkedIn Learning that challenge and inform you

documents.title: Developing Course AI Guidelines & Driving Class AI Discussion
documents.summary: DELTA article for instructors on writing course and assignment AI statements, with three sample statements, questions to consider and discussion activities. It states there is no official university AI policy.
documents.stance_why: The page says "there is no official university policy regarding AI use" and tells instructors to write their own course- and assignment-level guidelines. It offers three sample statements spanning restrictive to collaborative, so it sets tiers/templates and the stance is delegates.

units.why: "provide students with guidance on how you expect them to use AI tools" tells instructors to state expectations; P09.
units.anchor: It is important to provide students with guidance on how you expect them to use

units.why: "design concrete, actionable instructions for students on how and when they can use AI" asks instructors for specific course-level rules (P09).
units.anchor: design concrete, actionable instructions for students on how and when they can use AI

units.why: "design the procedures together" suggests co-creating AI rules with students (P67).
units.anchor: discuss AI use and expectations with students and design the procedures together

units.why: "clearly specify how AI may or may not be used in coursework, assignments, and assessments" requires explicit statements per work type (P09).
units.anchor: clearly specify how AI may or may not be used in coursework, assignments, and assessments

units.why: "provide examples and directions on how students should document and share their use of AI" asks instructors to set up disclosure; closest P24.
units.anchor: provide examples and directions on how students should document and share their use of AI
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors: they must tell students how to document and share AI use; disclosure itself is not mandated.

units.why: "there is no official university policy regarding AI use" is the document key fact: the decision is left to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: there is no official university policy regarding AI use
units.fit_note: States absence of a university policy, which is why the decision rests with instructors.

units.why: "align any statement with the same spirit of academic integrity" ties course statements to existing university integrity policy (P77).
units.anchor: align any statement with the same spirit of academic integrity

units.why: "Assignment-level guidance is often more helpful to students" recommends per-assignment rules (P04).
units.anchor: Assignment-level guidance is often more helpful to students.

units.why: "review the approved AI tools and data sensitivity levels" points instructors to vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: please review the approved AI tools and data sensitivity levels

units.why: "policies/statements for each assignment rather than an overall policy" suggests per-assignment rules (P04).
units.anchor: You may want to consider having policies/statements for each assignment rather than an overall policy.

units.why: "Some instructors simply consider AI use to fall under the general academic integrity guidelines" notes an option of using existing integrity rules (P77).
units.anchor: Some instructors simply consider AI use to fall under the general academic integrity guidelines

units.why: Sample "Highly Restricting" statement: "You are not allowed to use any artificial intelligence (AI) tools... to complete any part of your assignments" is a default ban (P01).
units.anchor: You are not allowed to use any artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "You are expected to do your own work" in the restricting statement makes students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: You are expected to do your own work and cite any sources you use properly.

units.why: "Any attempt to use these tools will be considered academic misconduct" classifies use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Any attempt to use these tools will be considered academic misconduct

units.why: "please consult with the instructor before submitting your work" is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: please consult with the instructor before submitting your work

units.why: Sample "Learning Aid" statement: "This course permits you to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools... as long as you do so in an ethical and responsible manner" is a conditional default permit (P02).
units.anchor: This course permits you to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "AI is more like your tutor or TA" allows AI as a tutor but not a replacement for thinking (P12).
units.anchor: AI is more like your tutor or TA, not a replacement for your independent thinking.

units.why: "Not use AI tools to replace your own thinking or analysis" keeps the student as thinker (P32).
units.anchor: Not use AI tools to replace your own thinking or analysis or to avoid engaging

units.why: "Cite or explain any AI tools you use" requires disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: Cite or explain any AI tools you use.

units.why: "the name of the AI tool, the date of access, the URL of the interface, and the specific prompt" lists citation details (P25).
units.anchor: the name of the AI tool, the date of access, the URL of the interface

units.why: "Explain what you learned from the AI tool, how you verified its accuracy" asks for a reflection on AI use (P26); no transcript is required.
units.anchor: Explain what you learned from the AI tool, how you verified its accuracy and reliability
units.fit_note: A written explanation or reflection, not a transcript or log.

units.why: "You are accountable for any mistakes or errors made by the AI tool" makes students own submitted work (P29).
units.anchor: You are accountable for any mistakes or errors made by the AI tool.

units.why: "Always check and edit the output before submitting your work" requires verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: Always check and edit the output before submitting your work.

units.why: "notify the instructor immediately and correct them" sets a duty to correct after submission; no type covers this, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: notify the instructor immediately and correct them as soon as possible
units.uncovered_note: After submission, a student who finds AI errors must tell the instructor and correct them.

units.why: "copying or paraphrasing the output without citation or transparency" makes nondisclosure a violation, so P28 (not P36, which is covered next).
units.anchor: copying or paraphrasing the output without citation or transparency

units.why: "is considered a form of academic dishonesty" classifies improper AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: is considered a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: "will result in a zero grade for the assignment and possible disciplinary action" states a concrete penalty (P37).
units.anchor: will result in a zero grade for the assignment and possible disciplinary action

units.why: "Some instructors will also list specific acceptable and unacceptable uses" notes instructors may itemize uses (P04).
units.anchor: Some instructors will also list specific acceptable and unacceptable uses

units.why: Sample "Collaborative Tool" statement: "students are encouraged to explore and utilize generative AI tools" is a default encourage (P02).
units.anchor: students are encouraged to explore and utilize generative AI tools

units.why: "valuable for brainstorming, drafting, and enhancing your understanding" names brainstorming and drafting as good uses (P15).
units.anchor: These tools can be valuable for brainstorming, drafting, and enhancing your understanding of the material.
units.fit_note: Also lists drafting and understanding the material, not only brainstorming.

units.why: "critically assess and cite any AI-generated content" requires citation (P24).
units.anchor: critically assess and cite any AI-generated content used in your assignments and projects
units.fit_note: Pairs citation with critically assessing the content.

units.why: "demonstrate their own understanding and critical thinking in their final submissions" keeps students as the thinkers (P32).
units.anchor: Students are expected to demonstrate their own understanding and critical thinking in their final submissions.

units.why: "We may also integrate AI Tools into some of our assignments" signals redesigning assignments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: We may also integrate AI Tools into some of our assignments.

units.why: "Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning" limits use by learner level; nearest is P42, which is about protecting novices.
units.anchor: Use AI tools only for tasks that are appropriate for your level of learning and
units.fit_note: Leaves the judgment of what suits the student level to the student; no stated novice rationale.

units.why: "following the citation style specified by the instructor" requires AI citation in an instructor-set style (P24).
units.anchor: following the citation style specified by the instructor

units.why: "Provide evidence of how you used the AI tool" requires documentation of use (P26).
units.anchor: Provide evidence of how you used the AI tool and how it contributed to your
units.fit_note: Evidence form is unspecified; need not be a transcript.

units.why: "Do not rely on the AI tool to produce flawless or correct results" warns that AI output can be wrong (P31).
units.anchor: Do not rely on the AI tool to produce flawless or correct results.

units.why: "discuss the use of AI tools with your group members and agree on how you plan to use them" is a group-level agreement rule that fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: discuss the use of AI tools with your group members and agree on how you
units.uncovered_note: Group members must agree among themselves on AI use and on how to be transparent with the instructor.

units.why: The "Questions to Consider" ask whether the statement covers different assignment types; it prompts per-assignment rules (P04).
units.anchor: Does your statement cover different types of assignments

units.why: "ask students to verify or check sources of information used by an AI tool" prompts instructors to require verification (P31).
units.anchor: Do you want to ask students to verify or check sources

units.why: "consider representation in any AI responses" prompts instructors to raise bias with students (P53).
units.anchor: consider representation in any AI responses

units.why: "acknowledge, cite or share AI use and how/when should they do that" prompts instructors to decide on disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: acknowledge, cite or share AI use

units.why: "Try out AI each semester" advises instructors to learn what AI can do before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Try out AI each semester as it continues to improve and develop
units.fit_note: Also implies re-testing each semester because AI keeps changing.

units.why: "Different levels of AI use from encouraged to limiting to prohibiting" describes a tiered model from Minnesota (P05).
units.anchor: Different “levels” of AI use from encouraged to limiting to prohibiting

units.why: "summarizing for students at the beginning of the semester some of the positive uses... and the negatives" asks instructors to explain AI with students (P66).
units.anchor: Consider summarizing for students at the beginning of the semester

units.why: "creating some course norms and guidelines together" recommends co-creating course norms with students (P67).
units.anchor: creating some course norms and guidelines together

units.why: The discussion table lists "Gender and Racial Bias in AI" as a concern for class discussion (P53).
units.anchor: Gender and Racial Bias in AI

units.why: "copyright or intellectual property concerns with how AI systems are trained" names IP as a concern (P52).
units.anchor: copyright or intellectual property concerns with how AI systems are “trained.”
units.fit_note: Also names diminished human creativity.

units.why: "Lack of basic skill development" is named as a concern, the skill-shortcut rationale (P41).
units.anchor: Lack of basic skill development

units.why: "Conduct a structured debate where students present their points and counter-arguments" is an in-class activity for discussing AI (P66).
units.anchor: Conduct a structured debate where students present their points and counter-arguments.

documents.unit: Graduate School Handbook 3.6 Theses and Dissertations
documents.title: Graduate Handbook: Artificial Intelligence Policy for Dissertations and Theses
documents.summary: Graduate Handbook section on AI in theses and dissertations, plus the authorship statement requirement. It allows generative AI use with required documentation and discusses privacy, bias and detectors.
documents.stance_why: The section says "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism" and its guiding principle is that candidates "must document their use clearly and thoroughly", so AI is allowed for theses and dissertations on condition of disclosure.

units.why: "propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically" states the purpose of the section (P56).
units.anchor: propose a framework to allow our graduate students to use these tools ethically

units.why: "calculators for words" frames LLMs by analogy with calculators; no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: LLMs are sometimes described as “calculators for words”
units.uncovered_note: Frames LLMs as calculators for words to set a tone for acceptance of use.

units.why: "Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools" states a Graduate School position favoring AI training (P70).
units.anchor: Our students would benefit from receiving training on how to use GAI tools efficiently, ethically
units.fit_note: A stated belief that students would benefit; no training is announced.

units.why: "The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism" says use alone is not misconduct; nearest P36, which it negates.
units.anchor: The mere use of LLMs does not constitute plagiarism
units.fit_note: Says mere use is not plagiarism, the opposite of classifying use as misconduct.

units.why: "poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs ... may constitute a form of plagiarism" makes inadequate disclosure the violation (P28).
units.anchor: poorly documented inclusion of outputs from LLMs into dissertations and theses may constitute a form

units.why: "must document their use clearly and thoroughly in their dissertation or thesis" is a mandatory disclosure rule (P24); P62 also fits but the rule is about disclosure.
units.anchor: Candidates utilizing GAI tools must document their use clearly and thoroughly
units.fit_note: Applies to dissertations and theses only.

units.why: "discuss ... acceptable use of LLMs or other GAI tools as early as practically possible with their advisor" is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: discuss general authorship principles and issues as well as acceptable use of LLMs

units.why: "Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use, and about the reasons" requires advisors to state rules and reasons; nearest P66.
units.anchor: Advisors need to be direct and transparent about what tools students are permitted to use
units.fit_note: Also covers stating which tools are permitted, not only explaining reasons.

units.why: "clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees" requires program-level AI principles to be communicated (P09).
units.anchor: they must be clearly communicated to the students and applied uniformly by advisory committees
units.fit_note: Concerns program-level principles and uniform application, not a syllabus statement.

units.why: "Material submitted can become part of the application database" warns of privacy and IP risks (P50).
units.anchor: Material submitted can become part of the application’s database

units.why: "inherent biases associated with them. Users must, at a minimum, be aware" requires awareness of bias (P53).
units.anchor: Users must, at a minimum, be aware of the existence of such issues.

units.why: "the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged" rejects detectors due to unreliability (P39).
units.anchor: the use of AI tools claiming to detect LLM generated text is discouraged

units.why: "no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper" is a research authorship rule (P62).
units.anchor: no LLM tool should be credited as co-author on a research paper
units.fit_note: Adds the reason: AI tools cannot take accountability for the work.

units.why: "does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses" sets scope and points to OFE and DELTA (P61).
units.anchor: does not directly address the use of GAI in generic courses
units.fit_note: Excludes ordinary courses and refers elsewhere, rather than defining AI.

units.why: "writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged" permits writing tools without disclosure (P18).
units.anchor: The use of writing assistance tools such as Grammarly is generally allowed and rarely acknowledged.

units.why: "If in doubt, students should contact their advisory committee and/or err on the side of caution and acknowledge use" is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: If in doubt, students should contact their advisory committee
units.fit_note: Also says to acknowledge use when in doubt.

units.why: "legislating all this to the n-th degree will not be possible because of the constant evolution of the tools" acknowledges the policy cannot be exhaustive (P54).
units.anchor: legislating all this to the n-th degree will not be possible
units.fit_note: Cites tool evolution and calls for judgment; no review schedule.

units.why: "Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is the broad category of AI capable of generating new data" defines GAI (P61).
units.anchor: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is the broad category of AI capable of generating new data

units.why: "Large Language Models (LLM) are a subset of GAI" defines LLMs (P61).
units.anchor: Large Language Models (LLM) are a subset of GAI

units.why: "Writing Assistant Tools are designed but not limited to checking spelling and grammar" defines the category exempted in practice (P61).
units.anchor: Writing Assistant Tools are designed but not limited to checking spelling and grammar

units.why: "A clear and thorough description of whether and how tools from Generative Artificial Intelligence were used" is a required part of the Authorship Statement (P24).
units.anchor: A clear and thorough description of whether and how tools from Generative Artificial Intelligence were
units.fit_note: Delivered as part of the Authorship Statement, which the advisory committee must approve.

notes: NC State has no official university-wide AI policy (DELTA says so as of May 2026). No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. The student page and DELTA article are guidance, not binding policy. The graduate handbook covers theses and dissertations only. Several units are instructor-directed prompts (DELTA questions to consider), coded with modality may/should and unit_stance neutral.
